definition: The inability of an ontology to include or encode every concept of interest to users of an ontology is known as the "content completeness problem".
details: The problem stems from the greater expressiveness of natural language relative to the finite enumeration of concepts present in an ontology. A specific instance of this problem may be temporarily resolved by adding missing concept/s to the target ontology, but this approach is not a general solution because in practice: There is a lag time between the appearance and usage of a concept in a domain and its incorporation into an ontology. In large ontologies it is difficult to know if the concept is already present Other workarounds to this problem include the use of post-coordination in ontologies (such as SNOMED CT) using free text or comment fields to supplement ontology entry systems. The first usage of the term "content completeness problem" was by Elkin, but it was described by Rogers and Rector in 1997.

explainer.lead: An ontology lists and encodes concepts, but people can express more ideas than that finite list contains. The content completeness problem is the resulting gap, which matters when users cannot find a concept they need or cannot tell whether it is already present.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a sticker album that is supposed to hold a sticker for every idea people want to discuss. New ideas and new ways of describing them keep appearing, so some stickers are always missing. You can add a missing sticker or write a note beside the others, but that does not make the album complete forever.
tiers.practitioner: When a required concept is absent, adding it can resolve that particular case, but incorporation lags behind the concept's appearance and use in the domain. In large ontologies, check carefully whether the concept already exists; post-coordination, as used in SNOMED CT, or free-text and comment fields in ontology entry systems can supplement encoded entries without providing a general cure.
tiers.paperLevel: Let U be the concepts of interest to users and C(O) the concepts encoded in ontology O; the problem occurs when U - C(O) is non-empty, reflecting natural language's greater expressiveness relative to finite enumeration. Elkin first used the term "content completeness problem", while Rogers and Rector described it in 1997. Adding individual missing concepts is not a general solution because incorporation lags and existing concepts can be difficult to locate in large ontologies.

explainer.example: A user working with SNOMED CT needs to record an idea for which no single encoded concept is available. They can post-coordinate existing concepts, or supplement the entry with free text or a comment, so the immediate record can be made even though the underlying completeness problem has not been eliminated.

usedIn.name: SNOMED CT
usedIn.detail: Post-coordination can combine existing concepts as a workaround when a needed concept is not directly encoded.

usedIn.name: Ontology entry systems
usedIn.detail: Free-text or comment fields can supplement an entry when the ontology does not cover everything users need to express.

usedIn.name: Large domain ontologies
usedIn.detail: Maintainers face delays in incorporating newly used concepts and difficulty determining whether a concept is already present.

explainer.intuition: Natural language can express more than an ontology's finite enumeration of concepts, so user needs can extend beyond what the ontology encodes.
howItWorks: A concept appears and comes into use within a domain.
Users look for that concept in the target ontology.
The concept may be absent, or its presence may be hard to establish in a large ontology.
Adding it fixes that instance, while post-coordination, free text, or comments can supplement the entry.
The general gap remains because new concepts and uses continue to appear before incorporation.
explainer.whyItMatters: Users may be unable to encode what they mean directly, and maintainers cannot make completeness permanent simply by adding each reported omission. Workarounds help individual entries but require awareness of incorporation delays and possible duplication.
misconceptions: Adding every currently reported missing concept is a general solution; it only resolves specific instances temporarily.
A failed search proves a concept is absent; in a large ontology, it can be difficult to know whether it is already present.
Post-coordination or free text makes the ontology complete; these are workarounds that supplement its entries.
